articles.title: At 83, Dave Obelkevich Will Run His 50th NYC Marathon. He Started by Accident.
articles.description:
Media credit : New York Road Runners
The first time Dave Obelkevich ran the New York City Marathon, he did not know he was in a race.
It was 1973, and he was jogging through Central Park when he noticed a cluster of runners wearing numbered bibs. He fell in behind them and tagged along for six miles.
By the time he looped back home, he had accidentally run most of the city's then-obscure road race. He signed up officially the following year.
Fifty-two years later, Obelkevich is 83 years old.
On Sunday, November 1, he will line up in Staten Island for his 50th finish of the New York City Marathon.
He is the only runner alive who has completed every five-borough edition of the race since the course expanded in 1976. His streak is unmatched.

The Streak That Started by Accident

Obelkevich ran his first official New York marathon in 1974. The race looped around Central Park and finished in just over four hours.
Two years later, race founder Fred Lebow pushed the course out through Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Manhattan. That 1976 race is the one Obelkevich never missed.
The 2020 edition was cancelled by the pandemic.
That cancellation is the only reason his streak sits at 49 going into Sunday rather than one higher.
Obelkevich is a retired New York City high school music teacher. He has played the violin since the third grade.
For 27 years he taught by day and ran at dawn before class.
Running fit around his life, not the other way around.

How Rare His Streak Really Is

The New York Road Runners track a club called "streakers," runners who have finished at least fifteen consecutive NYC Marathons. Hundreds of runners belong to that club.
Only Obelkevich's name is set to reach fifty.
Even inside the small world of ultra-endurance oddities, this is a staggering number. Britain's Ron Hill famously ran at least a mile a day for over 52 years in one of the longest unbroken streaks in distance running history.
Obelkevich's version is different. One race, one city, five decades.

The Numbers Behind 50 Finishes

In 1982, at age 39, Obelkevich ran his lifetime best in New York. He covered the 26.2-mile course in 2 hours and 40 minutes, averaging close to a six-minute mile.
From 1989 through 2014, he logged twenty-five consecutive sub-three-hour New York City Marathons. Twenty-five.
A single sub-three marathon is a bucket-list goal for most serious amateurs. Obelkevich stacked them for 25 straight years.
He has also finished the Boston Marathon eight times.
He stands five foot eight, lives on the Upper West Side, and still weighs roughly what he did in his racing prime.

What Masters Science Says About Lifelong Running

Lifelong aerobic exercise does something remarkable to the aging body. Peer-reviewed research on masters athletes suggests they are literally extending the known limits of human endurance.
That research shows VO2 max values and running economy in masters runners that outpace sedentary people half their age.
The physiology does not fully explain Obelkevich, but his consistency does.
He is not an outlier because he kept running.
He is an outlier because he kept racing, every single November, through injuries, grief, and a two-week ICU stay he once recovered from in time to still toe the line.

What Keeps Him Showing Up at 83

Age has reshaped his training.
He no longer stacks back-to-back 18-milers, and his weekly mileage is a fraction of what it was in his sub-three prime.
What has not changed is the ritual.
The alarm goes off, the gear comes out, and the ferry to Staten Island leaves before dawn.

The Mantra That Powers Every Mile

Obelkevich has a two-word phrase he repeats to himself in the late miles. "Keep going."
He has used it on the Queensboro Bridge, where the course goes silent and the crowd disappears. He has used it on First Avenue, when the quads start to lock up.
He has used it on cold years and hot years and injured years.
The mantra is small enough to fit inside the mind of an 83-year-old running his 50th marathon.

The Guide Who Runs Beside Him

Obelkevich's eyesight has faded enough that he no longer races alone.
For the past two years his guide has been a runner named Maria Finch, who trained specifically to pace him through the five boroughs.
Finch plans to run with him again on Sunday. She has said she keeps coming back because she understands how much the ritual still means to him.
The marathon is not his hobby. It is his calendar.

Why This Streak Matters for Older Runners

Running culture tends to lionize the elite marathoner who peaks in her twenties and disappears by 40.
Obelkevich's story is the better one, because the long game is a different sport entirely.
He joins a small roster of runners who treat marathons as a decades-long practice rather than a youthful goal.
Ed Whitlock set world masters records into his mid-eighties, and a growing share of the NYC field is now over 60.
The 2026 NYC Marathon drew a record 240,000 lottery applicants.
The fastest-growing age brackets in that pile of applications are the ones Obelkevich belongs to.
The data say running gets harder with age. Runners like Obelkevich say running gets different, not impossible.
Those are not the same thing.

What Sunday Looks Like for Dave Obelkevich

He will catch the ferry before sunrise.
He will stand in the Staten Island start village through the long cold wait that every NYC runner knows.
He will cross the Verrazzano into Brooklyn and feel the roar of the crowd carry him down Fourth Avenue. Finch will be beside him.
The pace will be slower than it used to be.
The finish line in Central Park will not be in doubt.
If he crosses it, and he intends to, Obelkevich will walk off having completed every five-borough New York City Marathon ever contested.
One race, one city, one ordinary runner who kept going for fifty years.
You do not have to be fast to be remarkable. You just have to keep showing up.

articles.title: A Son Pushed His Mother Through 21 Kilometres of Valencia, and the Guinness World Record Fell by a Minute
articles.description:
Pictures from Eric Domingo Roldán Instagram

The clock on the finish line read 1:15:49 when Eric Domingo Roldán crossed it at the Valencia Half Marathon on Sunday morning, pushing his mother Silvia in a manual wheelchair.

That time is a new Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon pushed with a person in a wheelchair, by a full minute.

A record that fell by sixty seconds

The previous mark, as the Guinness World Records organisation tracks it, had stood at 1:16:49.

Roldán cut it to 1:15:49 across the official 21.1 kilometres of the Medio Maratón de Valencia, a flat and famously fast course along the Turia riverbed.

His own Garmin showed 21.32 kilometres of distance covered at an average pace of 3:33 per kilometre.

Hold a 3:33 pace on your own two feet for a half marathon and you are already an elite club runner.

Hold it while pushing a loaded wheelchair, with the extra rolling resistance of a non-racing frame, and the achievement becomes something else entirely.

What Guinness actually requires

For the record to count, the wheelchair cannot be a sport specific racing chair with the tilted mag wheels you see in the Paralympic marathon field.

It has to be a standard manual wheelchair, closer to what someone might use day to day.

That rule is what makes the mark so hard to approach, let alone break.

Pushing a boxier, heavier chair at road racing pace is a bio-mechanical nightmare, as the runner has to maintain stride while absorbing the chair bumps and keeping it tracking straight on race-day road camber.

The person in the chair

Silvia Roldán, Eric mother, has lived with multiple sclerosis for more than twenty years.

MS is a progressive condition of the central nervous system in which the immune system attacks the protective myelin coating around nerve fibres, as Cleveland Clinic explains in its patient-facing primer.

For many people with MS, mobility becomes the first and most visible thing the disease takes away.

Silvia uses a wheelchair, and the simple reality of that fact is why Eric began racing with her in the first place.

A promise, now kept twice

This is not the first record the pair have set together.

Back in 2022, at the Valencia Marathon, Eric pushed Silvia across the full 42.195 kilometres in 2:52:39, breaking his own marathon Guinness mark set a year earlier at Barcelona.

That marathon record is still live.

Sunday October 25, 2026 added the half marathon equivalent to the family trophy case.

Why Valencia keeps being the venue

The Valencia Half Marathon is a World Athletics Elite Label event and part of the Superhalfs Series, which means it draws elite fields deep enough that the pacing out on course is honest from start to finish.

For a record attempt, that honest pacing matters as much as the course itself.

The course is pancake flat, the autumn weather is usually cool, and the organisation gives wheelchair push attempts the room they need in the early starting corrals.

None of that is accidental. Valencia has leaned into becoming a records track, and both the elite distance running world and the record-attempt world have taken notice.

Hyundai and the "Run to Progress" tie-in

The attempt was supported by Hyundai through its Run to Progress programme, the same Spanish mobility-and-sport platform that has backed Eric Roldán on past attempts.

The symbolism is on the nose, as a mobility brand backing a runner who refuses to let his mother lose her access to the road.

Hyundai also provided the family with transport from Barcelona to Valencia for the attempt.

Every detail of logistics matters when a record attempt is this tightly paced.

The emotional math

Eric wrote on Instagram after the finish that there are no words for what the pair had achieved.

He also wrote that he had done his job, for her, and for his mother, who is still his motivation.

The caption was in Spanish, and the sentiment translates cleanly to any language a runner reads in.

It is the same sentiment behind every charity marathon, every push rig at Boston, every parent who straps a stroller to their waist for a tempo run.

What this record raises

Eric has used every record attempt as a fundraiser for the Fundación Esclerosis Múltiple España, the Spanish Multiple Sclerosis Foundation.

His 2022 marathon record raised thousands of euros for MS research and patient services.

A record is the hook, and the money and the awareness are the real finish line.

If you are a runner reading this, Eric would almost certainly rather you donate to an MS charity than tell him he inspired you.

Visualizza questo post su Instagram

Un post condiviso da Eric Domingo Roldán 🐗 (@eeriic)

For runners in your own training

There is a reason stories like this one travel so far on running feeds.

They collapse two things that normally live apart in your training log, which is raw performance and raw purpose.

A 1:15:49 half marathon with a loaded wheelchair out front is a performance line in a Guinness ledger.

A son running for his mother is the reason you lace up at 5 a.m. on days you did not want to.

What to take away

If you want more context on the Spanish running tradition that produced athletes like Eric, we covered Reyes Estévez breaking the M45 record in Valencia earlier this season.

And if you want context on why Valencia has become the record factory of European distance running, we wrote about the prize structure and record payouts the Valencia Marathon now offers.

The small print of race calendars does matter. A fast, flat, well-marshalled course is why a mother and son from Barcelona now hold two Guinness World Records, one for each road distance that matters.

The finish

The record will not stand forever.

Someone, someday, will break 1:15:49 pushing a wheelchair over the half marathon.

But for now, on a sunny Sunday morning in Valencia, a Spanish amateur runner lowered the fastest-ever time by a full minute, with his mother riding in front of him, and raised a little more awareness for a disease that quietly steals mobility from millions of people worldwide.

That is a result worth bookmarking.

articles.title: A New Zealand Lawyer Just Ran an Ultramarathon Every Day for 1,000 Days, and the Numbers Behind It Are Absurd
articles.description:
Media Credit: Photos4sale

Shannon-Leigh Litt is a 47-year-old criminal defence lawyer from Whangārei, New Zealand.

On Saturday, September 27, 2026, she completed her 1,000th consecutive ultramarathon, a Guinness World Record that is ten times the previous women's mark.

She ran at least 51 kilometres every day since January 1, 2024.

Through nine countries, three bouts of severe flu, floods, and 40-plus degree heat, she never missed a day.

She went through more than 90 pairs of shoes and covered over 51,000 kilometres in the process.

The Training Math Is Not What You Think

Most runners assume a streak like this must be built on huge weekly mileage banked in advance. It was not.

Litt came in with 20 years of distance running behind her and ultra results as far back as 2010.

In November 2023, weeks before the streak began, she won the New Zealand 100K championship in 8:29:05, one of the fastest times ever by a New Zealand woman.

That base matters. Not because it gave her extra fitness to burn, but because it gave her a body that already knew how to metabolise 50 kilometres as a routine load rather than a peak effort.

The 51 versus 50 rule

Guinness requires a minimum of 50 kilometres to count as an ultra. Litt ran 51 every single day.

The extra kilometre is not vanity.

It is a buffer against GPS discrepancy, which she would need to submit for record ratification.

One short reading on one watch could invalidate a full day.

Small buffers compound. Over 1,000 days, that is an extra 1,000 kilometres, roughly a full month of running, spent on insurance.

The 1 am start problem

Litt often started her run at 1 or 2 in the morning so she could finish before her legal caseload started.

That is a specific kind of load nobody talks about in ultra literature.

The circadian cost of running that early day after day is significant.

Sleep deprivation, disrupted core temperature, and elevated cortisol are the predictable trio.

Research on chronic sleep restriction links it directly to impaired glucose regulation and reduced endurance capacity.

She did it anyway. And she still had to appear in court.

Learn More About The Method →

Limited-time reader discount available

What Actually Breaks First

Every experienced coach will tell you the joints go first.

In Litt's case, they did not go first. Illness did.

She reported three battles with severe flu in the final year of the streak.

Those were the hardest days to push through, and they are also the honest signal of what a body does under this load.

The immune system is the canary

Chronic high-volume endurance training suppresses immune function in a way most recreational runners never encounter.

The cortisol, the caloric deficit, and the disrupted sleep all combine to make you more likely to catch whatever is going around, and to catch it harder.

You can train through a lot. You cannot train around a virus.

If Litt had missed one day to a fever, the record was over.

That is why illness, not cartilage, is the first real threat in these streaks.

The verification cost

Guinness wanted video from the start and finish of every one of the 1,000 days.

Photos from the course. The word of two witnesses.

GPS data from two watches worn at once.

Litt reportedly approached 11 people in Europe before finding one willing to witness a run.

That is not a training cost. It is a paperwork cost, and it is the reason why almost nobody attempts records at this length.

Where This Sits in the Streak-Running Pantheon

The previous women's record was 200 consecutive days, held by Colorado's Candice Burt.

Litt took it to 1,000. That is a five-times jump, in a discipline where records usually move by single-digit percentages.

For context, the running-every-day streak of British legend Ron Hill lasted 19,032 days, but Hill's streak required only one mile per day.

Litt's daily minimum was fifty times that.

The nearest ongoing effort is a former rugby pro attempting 100 ultramarathons in 100 days, an impressive project on its own terms and yet one-tenth of what Litt has just finished.

What she is doing next

Litt has already hinted at a complete change for the next year, with new hobbies.

Guinness has reportedly reached out about another marathon record they could verify.

Whatever comes next, her long-term recovery from this effort will itself be a case study.

Research on ultra-endurance athletes shows measurable cardiac remodelling after sustained high-volume training.

Watching what happens to her resting heart rate and body composition over the next 12 months will teach the sport something new.

The Lesson for the Rest of Us

You do not need to run an ultra a day to learn from this streak.

The three transferable lessons are the ones almost every runner underrates: illness is a bigger threat than injury, sleep is a bigger training variable than mileage, and small buffers compound.

Litt built a buffer of one kilometre a day and it saved her record.

What buffer are you building in your own week?

articles.title: Natalie Villalobos Finished the 70.3 World Championship at 21 Weeks Pregnant With an Ultrasound in Her Hand
articles.description:
Pictures from IRONMAN Triathlon, Instagram

Natalie Villalobos, a 29-year-old American triathlete, crossed the finish line of the 2026 IRONMAN 70.3 World Championship in Nice, France at 21 weeks pregnant.

She covered the 1.2-mile swim, the 56-mile ride through the hills above the Côte d'Azur, and the 13.1-mile run along the Promenade des Anglais in 8 hours, 9 minutes, 48 seconds, then held an ultrasound photo of her daughter above her head as she entered the chute.

She had qualified for the race one month before she found out she was pregnant.

A qualifier earned, a positive test one month later

Villalobos is a certified pre- and postnatal fitness specialist who had been racing long-course triathlon for several seasons.

In March 2026 she locked in her slot for the 70.3 World Championship. In April, she took a pregnancy test and it came back positive.

That same month, while already in her first trimester, she completed a full IRONMAN (2.4-mile swim, 112-mile bike, full marathon) in 12 hours, 36 minutes, 44 seconds.

Across the summer, she documented every training week on Instagram: the belly growth beside the bike fit changes, the slower long runs, the reduced heat exposure, and the ongoing clearance from her obstetrician.

What the 70.3 Worlds course asks of any athlete

The 2026 IRONMAN 70.3 World Championship was held on October 12, 2026, in Nice, with a 1.9-kilometer swim in the Mediterranean, a 90-kilometer ride into the hills above the city, and a 21.1-kilometer run on the seafront.

The bike is the hard part. The course climbs away from the coast through the villages of the Alpes-Maritimes, with ramps that touch 12 percent gradient and almost 1,500 meters of elevation gain.

That profile is already a stiff ask for a non-pregnant qualifier. Carrying a second-trimester bump through it is a different problem again.

Villalobos told followers the added weight on the climbs and the shifting center of gravity on technical descents were the two biggest adjustments she had to make.

How her race day actually broke down

She swam the 1.9 kilometers in warm water with the age-group waves, took a controlled transition, and settled into an endurance pace on the bike with heart rate as her primary gauge rather than power.

On the run she walked the aid stations, drank at every one, and kept effort below conversational threshold. She crossed the mat in 8:09:48, then held her baby's ultrasound photo above her head for the finish-line camera.

What the science actually says about racing through pregnancy

The headline is dramatic. The underlying guidance is not new.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) updated its position in 2020 and recommends that healthy pregnant women accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, and that athletes who were already active before pregnancy can continue, including running, with obstetric clearance.

Published guidance makes a clear point: when there are no complications, physical activity in pregnancy is safe and carries measurable benefits. For a referenced overview, see the MotherToBaby exercise fact sheet on NIH Bookshelf.

The caveats that matter for an endurance athlete still apply, hard. Contact sports, altitude above 6,000 feet, scuba diving, and anything with a meaningful fall risk are off the table.

The 70.3 bike leg in Nice is a controlled closed-road course. Villalobos rode it as a steady endurance effort, not as a race.

Why qualifying before you know changes the calculation

Villalobos earned her slot the way every age-grouper does, by racing a qualifier at a fitness level that reflected months of specific training.

Her baseline aerobic engine was already there when the pregnancy began. That matters, because ACOG and most sports-medicine physicians draw a bright line between maintaining prior activity and initiating a new high-volume habit mid-pregnancy.

A trained athlete finishing a long race she had already prepared for sits firmly in the first category. A sedentary person signing up for a half-iron in the second trimester would not.

The physical adjustments she talked openly about

A few concrete changes showed up again and again in her training logs.

Pace by effort, not by watch. On every run she let heart rate and perceived exertion drive the session instead of goal pace.

Shorter long runs. Weekly long-run volume was capped and broken up, with walk breaks built in.

More fueling, more hydration. Pregnancy raises resting metabolic rate and blood volume, and she ate and drank well above her pre-pregnancy race-day baseline.

Pelvic floor and core work twice a week. This was non-negotiable for her as a prenatal fitness specialist, because long-distance running loads the pelvic floor every single step.

What this looks like for a non-elite runner

The Villalobos race is not a template. It is an extreme case built on years of base, specialist knowledge, and medical oversight.

For most pregnant runners already in a routine, the practical version of the same approach is simpler. Keep moving, hold effort in the easy-conversational range, drop goal paces, respect your obstetrician's calls, and get a pelvic floor assessment early in the second trimester.

If you want a sense of how far a running base will carry into pregnancy with the right structure, read how Ali Anderson ran a 2:59 marathon at eight months pregnant in Sydney.

Discover the authentic training methods of Kenyan runners and start improving your running faster than you ever thought possible.

Learn More About The Method →

Limited-time reader discount available

What a pregnant mother's training may give the baby

There is a parallel research thread worth knowing about if the Villalobos finish line is making you reconsider training through pregnancy.

Recent work in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise points to a mechanism called fetal programming, where the physical activity of a pregnant mother appears to influence the developing baby's vascular and mitochondrial density in utero.

That evidence is covered in more detail in our write-up of the mitochondrial inheritance research, and it reframes the pregnancy-training conversation away from pure risk management and toward something closer to a shared adaptation.

The ultrasound at the finish line

The image that spread across triathlon social media was simple. A woman holding a prenatal ultrasound of her daughter above her head on the Promenade des Anglais, visor on, race bib 1468 pinned to the chest of her trisuit.

The caption on the repost that went viral read talk about a race-day buddy. The comments were a mix of applause and alarm, which is the typical shape of any public conversation about elite exercise and pregnancy.

The medical consensus Villalobos operated inside of is the quieter story under the headline. It is also the one worth reading twice.

articles.title: Zion Just Became the First US National Park to Own an All-Terrain Wheelchair, and Every Other Park Is Now Behind
articles.description:
Zion National Park, in the red-rock canyon country of southwest Utah, has quietly become the first US national park to own an all-terrain wheelchair for free public use.
The chair sits at the Zion Canyon Visitor Center, free to borrow for a day, no reservation, no fee.
Sixteen trails that were closed to standard wheelchairs are now open. That is not a marketing line.
It is a policy shift with real consequences for adaptive athletes, and for the trail runners who guide them.

What Zion Actually Did

The chair itself is an Extreme Motus, a manual off-road wheelchair with oversized tyres built for sand, rock, and uneven ground.
It was funded through a donation from the nonprofit 2LIV4 to the Zion Forever Project.
Other national parks have offered adaptive gear before, but through nonprofit partners on a seasonal loan.
Zion is the first park to own the equipment outright, list it on the NPS website, and maintain it in-house.
The distinction matters. Owned equipment stays year-round.
It shows up in official park literature. It is not a pilot that quietly ends when a partner's grant runs out.

The rules for using it

You visit the Zion Canyon Visitor Center information desk. There is one chair.
It is first-come, first-served, and reservations are not accepted.
The chair is roughly six feet long, too big for the park shuttle.
So the park hands borrowers a driving pass for the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive, a road otherwise closed to private vehicles for most of the year.
That pass is not a small gesture. In a park that guards that road carefully, it is a statement.

Why This Matters to the Running Community

This is not just a wheelchair story. It is a terrain access story, and terrain access is exactly what trail runners think about every day.
Adaptive endurance is already a bigger movement than most road runners realise.
Guided racers, sighted-guide runners, and push-athletes have been quietly stitching together their own access for years.
Team Hoyt built a template that took decades to normalise, and even now most race directors are still catching up.

The runner who will push, and the runner who will guide

Talk to anyone who has raced with a push-chair partner and the same word comes up: permission.
The runner in the chair needs a course that will physically let them through.
The runner pushing needs equipment that will not disintegrate on the third mile.
Zion just gave both of them a permission slip on 16 trails.
For a trail runner who has ever wanted to spend a day showing a family member, a client, or a friend a canyon floor they had written off as inaccessible, the calculation has changed.

The Sixteen Trails, and What They Actually Open Up

Zion designates 16 trails as suitable for the Extreme Motus.
The full list is on the NPS accessibility page, and the highlights speak for themselves.
Two are already paved: the Pa'rus Trail and the Riverside Walk.
The Pa'rus is a favourite of masters runners looking for a flat, forgiving surface at altitude.
Lower Emerald Pools and Weeping Rock are the two that the chair really unlocks.
These are the terrain profiles that turn away standard wheelchairs and small strollers.

What is still off-limits

The chair is not for the Angels Landing chains section. It is not for the Zion Narrows.
These are climbing and canyoneering routes, not trails, and no all-terrain chair changes that.
The park is being honest about the ceiling. That honesty is part of what makes the program credible.

What Runners Can Take From This

There is a pattern in adaptive athletics that shows up in almost every profile of a long-serving guide or push-partner.
They stop measuring the run by pace. They start measuring it by what got opened.
That mindset is contagious in a good way.
A trail run stops being about your split and starts being about the terrain itself, about who could and could not have made it up that ridge, about who might make it now.
For a taste of what this looks like at the elite end of the sport, see how Sally McRae threw up for eight hours and still took third at a 200-mile ultra.
The same refusal to accept limits shows up at the 71-year-old grandmother who is outperforming most 20-somethings in HYROX after treating cancer as another obstacle.

The pressure this puts on other parks

Zion just made a move that costs one wheelchair, one visitor-center storage plan, and one policy update.
The bill for going second is now lower, because Zion already proved the operational model.
The bill for going last is now a lot higher, because the story is out.
Expect a slow trickle, then a rush. Watch how quickly the next park announces a similar program in 2027.

The Bigger Picture

Adaptive endurance is having a moment.
Between the Zion program, the growing prominence of guided trail events, and the enduring legacy of Team Hoyt, the definition of a runner keeps quietly widening.
That widening is worth celebrating from inside the running community, not just observing from outside it.
Every runner who has ever guided a blind athlete on a road race, every parent who has pushed a stroller up a park hill, every pacer who has adjusted their stride so a friend could finish, is part of the same continuity.
Zion just made that continuity a little easier to see. And a lot easier to reach.

articles.title: Contact Lost With British Adventurer Ash Dykes During Congo Basin Expedition
articles.description:
Photo credit: Ash Dykes/PR Hunter
Welsh adventurer Ash Dykes has gone quiet in one of the most remote places on Earth.
On Wednesday, October 21, his support team said it had heard nothing from Dykes or his crew for more than 16 hours, describing the gap as concerning.
There is no confirmation that anyone is hurt or in danger. The team has not said where the group last checked in or what might be behind the blackout.

What Is Known So Far

The update went out on Dykes' official social channels, signed by a support team member named Matt.
It promised more information as soon as the team hears from the expedition.
Dykes, 35, is paddling an inflatable kayak down the Sangha River in the Congo Basin.
He set off on October 8 alongside filmmaker Will Pérez and their guide, Obed Temba.
The route covers more than 700 kilometres (about 435 miles), from Nola in the Central African Republic to Mossaka in the Republic of the Congo.
The whole trip was expected to take three to four weeks.
The North Wales Daily Post reports that his own website calls the region one of the last true wildernesses left on the planet. Crocodiles, hippos, tropical disease and punishing heat are all part of the risk, and Dykes had already posted about a painful sting from an unidentified insect.

How the Expedition Was Going Before the Silence

Dykes had been posting regular videos from the river, showing raw day-to-day conditions rather than polished travel content.
Around day 14, he shared a clip walking through the challenges the team was facing.
The trip had not started smoothly either.
Reports note logistical setbacks before the crew even reached the water at Nola.
His choice of an inflatable kayak sparked plenty of debate online, with many followers worried it left the team exposed to large wildlife.
Dykes has argued the opposite, telling Paddling Magazine that the boats can take hits from sharp rocks and branches and still keep the journey moving.
The project is built around taking people along in near real time.
That is also why a gap of a single day landed so heavily with his large online audience.

Before He Paddled, He Walked

The kayak is new territory for many of his followers, but his reputation was built on foot.
That is why so many runners and endurance athletes track every update.

Mongolia, 2014

In his early twenties, he became the first recorded person to cross Mongolia solo and unsupported, covering roughly 1,500 miles in 78 days.
He dragged a trailer weighing around 120 kilograms behind him the whole way.

Madagascar, 2016

He then trekked about 1,600 miles through Madagascar's interior in 155 days, climbing the island's eight highest mountains en route. He contracted malaria during the journey and kept going.

The Yangtze, 2018 to 2019

His best-known feat took 352 days.
He became the first person to walk the roughly 4,000-mile length of China's Yangtze River, a journey that made him a household name in China.
More recently, he completed a source-to-sea paddle through the interior of Suriname for the documentary Uncharted Amazon.
The Congo trip is Mission 01 of Project 6, a plan for six expeditions in six extreme environments over about 12 months, according to his Wikipedia profile and expedition coverage.

Why 16 Hours of Silence Is Not the Same as an Emergency

Expedition communications in dense rainforest are fragile.
Satellite devices need open sky and charged batteries, and a thick canopy, storms or a long day on the water can all delay a check-in.
That is exactly why serious teams agree on check-in windows before anyone leaves home.
A missed window does not mean disaster, but it does mean the people at base start working through a plan that was agreed in advance.
The support team's message reflected that balance.
It flagged real concern without speculating, and it asked followers to be patient.
Photo credit: Ash Dykes

The Lesson for Every Runner Who Heads Out Alone

You do not need to be crossing the Congo Basin for this to apply to you.
Long solo trail runs, remote ultra course recces and pre-dawn road miles all carry a smaller version of the same risk.

Leave a route and a worry time

Tell someone exactly where you are going and when you expect to be back.
Then agree on the moment they should stop waiting and start calling.

Carry a way to reach people beyond cell coverage

On remote trails, a two-way satellite messenger can send a check-in or an SOS where phones fail.
It is the same basic tool expedition teams rely on.

Protect your power

A dead battery turns a minor delay into a genuine scare for the people waiting on you.
Carry a small power bank on long days and switch your phone to low-power mode early.

Agree in advance what silence means

Decide how many missed check-ins should trigger action, and who takes it.
A clear plan stops your support person from panicking too early or waiting far too long.

Keep your check-ins short, boring and regular

A two-word message at the same points on every run is worth more than a long update once a day.
Regular, predictable contact makes it obvious, fast, when something has actually changed.
Agree on the format too, whether that is a preset satellite message or a quick text with your location.
The less thinking a check-in takes, the more likely you are to send it when you are tired.
Cody Taylor's 17 days alone on Vermont's Long Trail shows how much planning goes into time spent far from help.
If you are weighing whether to train solo at all, it is also worth reading why running with a partner can make you faster.
Heat is the other quiet danger on any long, remote effort.
The warning signs in this guide to preventing heat stroke while running apply whether you are on a Kentucky road or a tropical riverbank.

What Comes Next

For now, the honest answer is that nobody outside the expedition knows what has caused the silence.
Across earlier journeys, Dykes has come through malaria, a pack of wolves trailing him in China and near heat stroke in the Gobi.
About two weeks into a journey planned for three to four weeks, a long stretch of the Sangha still lies between the team and Mossaka.
Whatever comes next, the support crew at home will be the first to know.
His team has promised updates as soon as there is news.
We will update this story when contact is restored.

articles.title: A Polish Runner Who Started in Her 50s Died Weeks Before Her 90th Birthday
articles.description:
Media from sportgdansk
Janina Rosińska, a Polish runner who took up competitive running in her 50s, has died at the age of 89.
Her life is one of the clearest examples you will find of how late a serious running career can begin.
The retired geography teacher from Pabianice, in central Poland, drew press attention in April.
She raced at the European Masters Athletics Championships in Toruń, and her run was covered in Polish and international reporting.

A 200 metre race weeks before her 90th birthday

The 15th European Masters Athletics Championships Indoor took place in Toruń from 27 March to 2 April 2026.
According to TVP World's report on the race, Rosińska was the only athlete in the 85 and over age group and completed the 200 metres in 61 seconds.
That race fell just weeks before her 90th birthday.
The same report says she ran with a pacemaker, which makes the effort more striking.
Because she was the only entrant in her category, she did not beat a rival for the title.
What she did was finish the distance at 89 in a championship, and that is the achievement worth keeping in view.

Why age group racing works this way

Masters championships group athletes into five-year age bands, so the oldest categories often have very few entrants.
An athlete in the 85 and over band can be the only competitor on the track.
For a runner in that band, the real test is making the start line.
Rosińska made it at 89, an age when most people have stopped racing.
Masters athletics also lets runners measure progress against their own age group rather than against much younger athletes.
For many people who start late, that comparison is more useful than a comparison with the fastest runners on the course.
That is part of why results in these categories attract attention.
A single race can show what an older body can still do, and it gives other people a reason to test their own limits.

She did not start competitive running until her 50s

Rosińska was never a career athlete.
She began training seriously for competitive running when she was well into her 50s, an age when many people assume their competitive years are behind them.
That timing matters if you are starting late yourself.
A late start does not have to be a small one, and her record shows how much racing a person can build after the usual window has closed.
Late starters often face doubts from friends, family and themselves, and the story of a runner who began in her 50s answers many of those doubts at once.
You do not need to match her record to take the lesson, which is that the starting point can be set by the day you decide to begin.

More than 360 marathons and 800 medals

Press coverage of her career reports that she completed more than 360 marathons and earned over 800 medals across several distances.
Those totals come from reports rather than an official database, so treat them as reported figures.
The University of the Third Age in Łask, an organization she was part of, said her medals reflected her perseverance and the joy she took from being active.
Its account puts the emphasis on the habit rather than the trophies.

What her community remembered

The Łask group described her as full of energy, cheerfulness and inner strength.
It also said that her greatest passion was running, and that she kept proving what was possible.
One line from its farewell stands out.
The group said she showed that it is never too late to fulfil one's dreams.

Lessons for runners who start late

Her story is not a training plan, but it points to habits that matter for anyone starting or returning to running later in life.
The four points below draw on her record and on how her community described her.
  • Start with the body you have. Rosińska began serious training in her 50s, so age alone did not close the door on competition.
  • Build for the long haul. Her record includes sprinting and marathon racing, which shows that a running life can cover more than one distance.
  • Let the medals follow the habit. Her community linked her trophies to her joy in being active, not to one peak result.
  • Keep showing up to the start line. Her Toruń race came at 89, weeks before her 90th birthday, so showing up mattered more than her age on the day.

Other late starts worth reading

Her story sits alongside other examples of runners who found their stride late.
For a comparison in competition, read this profile of a grandmother who is outperforming many younger athletes in HYROX.
If you want the broader case for training at any age, start with why age is just a number when it comes to running.
It argues that age is a smaller barrier to running than many people expect.

What the record does and does not show

The championship itself is well documented, with official results published online.
It is a major event on the European masters calendar, and one podcast summary of the event reported more than 3,500 athletes from more than 15 countries.
Her 61 second sprint and her marathon totals rest on press reports, so read them as reported figures rather than audited records.
Her story is strongest as an example of late-life commitment, not as a statistical benchmark.
Focus on what is consistent across the record, which is a race at 89, a championship entry, and a community that described her energy and commitment in the same terms. That combination is more useful to you than any single headline figure.

Remembering Janina Rosińska

Rosińska was 89 when she raced in Toruń, weeks before her 90th birthday.
Her community remembers her as a runner who started late, kept going, and showed others that a competitive life does not have to end early.

articles.title: “When I Am Running, My Disability Seems to Disappear” - A Father Pushed His Son Through 32 Boston Marathons
articles.description:
Picture Credit : AP Photo/Michael Dwyer
In 1977, a 15-year-old boy with cerebral palsy in Massachusetts asked his father to push him in a five-mile charity race for a paralysed lacrosse player.
That evening, using a computer that let him spell one letter at a time by tapping his head, the boy typed a single sentence.
"Dad, when I am running, my disability seems to disappear."
Everything Team Hoyt became, and everything the adaptive endurance world inherited from them, followed from that sentence.

The Boy Who Was Never Supposed to Speak

Rick Hoyt was born in 1962 with cerebral palsy after complications during birth.
Doctors told his parents, Dick and Judy, that he would be a vegetable for the rest of his life and recommended institutionalising him.
Fifty years later, Dick would famously joke that he and Rick were still trying to figure out what kind of vegetable.
The Hoyts refused the institution.
Engineers at Tufts University built Rick a communication device that let him spell words with head movements.
With it, he attended public school for the first time, and eventually earned a degree from Boston University.

The father who was not a runner

Dick Hoyt was 37 years old in 1977. He ran a couple of miles a week.
He was a National Guard officer, not an endurance athlete.
When Rick used his communication device to ask about the charity race, Dick said yes because he could not bear to say no to his son.
The pair finished next to last, in a wheelchair that a family member later described as maneuvering like a shopping cart with a bum wheel.
For the next two weeks, Dick could barely walk. He was, in his own words, disabled.

The Sentence That Changed Everything

That night, Rick sat in front of his communication device and typed the line that would define the next four decades of American road racing.
"Dad, when I am running, my disability seems to disappear."
For a boy who could not speak, could not walk, could not use his arms or legs, and had spent 15 years being seen through the lens of what he could not do, the run had erased the lens.
Dick Hoyt spent the rest of his life making sure that erasure kept happening.

The training a father did in a wheelchair

When Rick was at school and unable to train with him, Dick would put a bag of cement in the wheelchair and run alone.
That is how the man who barely ran a couple of miles a week became a marathoner and eventually a triathlete.
That detail is not the flashy part of the Team Hoyt story. It is the real one.
The cement bag, done in private, when nobody was watching, is what made the finish lines possible.

The 32 Bostons, the 6 Ironmans, and the 1,100 Races

Team Hoyt went on to compete in over 1,100 endurance events, including 72 marathons, 257 triathlons, 6 full Ironman triathlons, and 32 Boston Marathons.
Their first Boston was 1980. Race organisers turned them down twice in the late 1970s and eventually told them they would need to earn a qualifying time.
So they did.
Every one of those races involved Dick pushing, pulling, or towing Rick.
In the swims, Dick pulled Rick in a small boat with a rope tied around his waist.
On the bike, Rick sat in a special seat over the front wheel. On the run, the specialised racing chair did the carrying.

The 2013 finish that never happened

Dick had planned to retire from Boston after the 2013 race. That was the year of the finish-line bombing.
The Hoyts were about a mile out when officials stopped them.
They came back in 2014 for one more, and finished properly.
Full details of the return year and the bombing are on the Boston Globe's obituary of Rick Hoyt.
Dick died in 2021 at 80. Rick died in 2023 at 61.
A dentist named Bryan Lyons pushed Rick for the years between Dick's retirement in 2014 and Lyons' own unexpected death in 2020.

Why That Sentence Still Matters

Rick Hoyt's single-sentence description of what running gave him is now the founding text of the entire modern adaptive endurance movement.
Every guided blind runner, every push-athlete duo, every wheelchair marathoner racing at a major, every all-terrain wheelchair now being loaned out at national parks, is downstream of that one line typed by head movements on an early computer in 1977.
The Boston Marathon just unveiled its 130th-running golden medal for 2026, and every runner who lines up on that course is running a race the Hoyts helped make more inclusive.
If you want to know how to watch the Boston Marathon, keep an eye on the push-athlete duos. They are the Hoyts' direct legacy.

What runners can still learn from Dick

Dick Hoyt was not a naturally gifted athlete.
He was a middle-aged man who said yes to his son, and then went home and put a bag of cement in a wheelchair to train.
The Team Hoyt lesson is not about talent. It is about response.
When the person you love asks you for something impossible, the useful question is not can they? but what would need to change to say yes?

What Rick left behind

Rick Hoyt used running to speak.
He said, through his father's legs, that a person is more than the sum of what their body cannot do.
You can read the full history of the family, the charity, and the race schedule at the Team Hoyt Foundation website.
The Hoyt Foundation still helps individuals with disabilities and the organisations that serve them.

The Sentence, One More Time

"Dad, when I am running, my disability seems to disappear."
One sentence. Forty-plus years of racing.
Thirty-two Bostons and six Ironmans.
Over a thousand finish lines, and a movement.
Nothing else in modern endurance sport has done more with fewer words.

articles.title: Danny Grossi Was Told He May Never Run Again, an Ontario Doctor Turned His Comeback Into a Software Company
articles.description:
Pictured from Danny Grossi

In an ICU bed in 2025, Danny Grossi, a doctor from Aurora, Ontario, was staring down the possibility of losing his leg.
A blood clot in his calf had triggered a cascade of complications, and doctors told him he might never run again.
In March 2026, less than a year later, he stood on top of the podium at the Canadian Indoor Masters Championships, having won the M55-59 1,500 meters in 5:07.84.
In between, he had also built a software company.

How this started

Grossi is not a career runner. He is a physician with degrees from Princeton University and the University of Toronto, and he had drifted away from competitive racing for decades.
In 2024, watching his four children compete on the track, he decided to come back.
He raced cross-country, started building fitness, and everything was going well until the numbness started.

The clot that hid in plain sight

During the 2024 cross-country season he began feeling numbness in his ankle and foot.
His doctors could not figure out what was causing it, and the symptoms dragged on into the spring.
By early 2025, as he was preparing for the Canadian Masters Indoor Championships, the pain became unbearable.
An extended scan finally caught it: a blood clot in his leg, higher up than the original imaging had reached.

The complication that almost took the leg

Once the clot was cleared, blood came flooding back into a lower leg that had been restricted for months.
That triggered compartment syndrome, a condition where pressure builds inside a muscle compartment and starts choking off the tissue from the inside.
It required four fasciotomies to relieve the pressure.
He spent 29 days in hospital, including eight in intensive care.

The question that changed everything

Grossi tells the story of a single question he asked himself while lying in that ICU bed.
If he was fortunate enough to run again, how would he rebuild intelligently?
That is the question most returning-from-injury runners never articulate.
They train harder, or they train softer, and hope the body responds.

Why a physician was well positioned to try something different

Grossi came at rehab the way a scientist would attack an unfamiliar problem. He tracked everything he could get a signal on: heart rate variability, training load, sleep, subjective effort, blood markers, cadence, pace.
Then he did the thing most runners never do with their own data.
He tried to make it mean something.

The AI experiment

Rather than pipe every metric into a spreadsheet and stare at it, he used artificial intelligence models to look for signal across the streams simultaneously.
He wanted the tools to tell him what was correlating with feeling good, and what was correlating with the next bad run.
The work he was doing on himself turned into a product.
That product is now called PIRX, short for Performance Intelligence Rx, and it is being marketed as a performance intelligence platform for runners.

The comeback race

In March 2026, Grossi returned to the Canadian Masters Indoor Championships he had been preparing for the previous year when the clot showed up.
He won.
5:07.84 in the M55-59 1,500 meters is not a token result. It is a legitimate championship-caliber time for that age group, and it came less than a year after the ICU.

The scale of what that took

Rebuilding from compartment syndrome and four fasciotomies is not a linear process.
Nerve function returns slowly and unpredictably, and calf strength has to be rebuilt from a base of essentially zero.
For any runner who has come back from a serious injury, the story will feel familiar.
Our guide on making a running comeback after time off covers the psychology of that process; Grossi just happened to add a research project on top.

The training-data angle nobody talks about

One of the most interesting details, quietly buried in the Canadian Running Magazine profile of Grossi's comeback, is the sheer volume of his historical training data. He had years of it, from before the injury.
That gave his AI experiment a baseline that most returning runners will never have.
When his return-to-run numbers looked off, he had comparison data going back years to check them against.

What this actually tells the rest of us

Most runners will not have Grossi's medical background, and most will not be building an AI training platform in their downtime.
That is fine, because his story still lands two useful points.

One: data only helps if you *use* it

Every runner reading this is probably wearing a watch that collects far more data than they ever look at.
Grossi's project only worked because he decided to interrogate his numbers instead of glancing at them.
That is a habit, not a technology. The tools help, but the habit is the hard part.

Two: the mental frame matters as much as the physical rebuild

Grossi has been open about the fact that he needed a project during his recovery.
The AI experiment was as much psychology as it was performance science.
For a related look at how age-group athletes stay ambitious through setbacks, our piece on training smarter in your 40s, 50s, and 60s sits comfortably next to Grossi's story.

What is next

Grossi is now training for the 2026 World Masters Athletics Championships, aiming to return to the international stage.
The PIRX platform he built during recovery is now the tool he is using to plan his own preparation.
In his own words, buried in the reporting: the irony is that the product only exists because everything went wrong.
That is a good line, and it lands right.
Most useful things get built by people who had no choice but to figure something out.
The masters running world tends to specialize in that particular kind of person.

articles.title: A World-Class Skyrunner Vanished on the Matterhorn 10 Days Ago. The Official Search Has Ended
articles.description:
Pictures from Kalie McCrystal, Instagram
Kalie McCrystal, a 38-year-old Canadian skyrunner and mountaineer from Squamish, British Columbia, has been missing on the Italian side of the Matterhorn since Tuesday, September 1.
She was last seen on her descent, moving smoothly, above the Jean-Antoine Carrel hut at 3,830 meters.
Italian search authorities suspended helicopter operations on September 4, and the official search was called off on September 8 after a week of aerial and ground sweeps.
As of this writing, ten days after she vanished, her family and the international skyrunning community are still hoping for news.

Who Kalie McCrystal is

McCrystal is not a beginner in high places.
She spent years as a corporate lawyer, then walked away from the profession to pursue serious mountain running full-time.
She has raced on the international Skyrunner World Series circuit, and her friends describe her as calm, precise, and unusually careful for a runner working at that level of technical exposure.

Skyrunning, briefly explained

Skyrunning is the discipline that sits at the border of ultrarunning and mountaineering.
Courses often exceed 2,000 meters of vertical, involve fixed-rope sections, exposed scrambles, and glaciated terrain.
It is not trail running in the conventional sense, and it is not casual mountaineering.
The best skyrunners move like climbers who happen to be running.

The route she was on

McCrystal was on the Lion Ridge, the standard climbing route up the Matterhorn from the Italian village of Cervinia.
It is a long, technical route with thousands of feet of drop on either side and sustained scrambling on rock.
She had summited the mountain by this same route in early August, and was scouting it in preparation for a formal speed record attempt.

What she was trying to do

McCrystal's September 1 outing was a reconnaissance run for a Fastest Known Time attempt, targeting the round trip from Cervinia to the summit and back down the Italian route.
According to the Outside Magazine report on her disappearance, the standing women's FKT on the route is 5 hours, 14 minutes, and 53 seconds, set by Karina Anderson on August 9. McCrystal wanted to run it in under five hours.

Why an FKT recon is not a light day out

An FKT attempt on a route like Lion Ridge is not a race you run cold.
Route familiarity is safety, because on technical mountain terrain a wrong line does not just cost minutes, it can cost everything.
That is exactly what she was doing on September 1.
She had been in Cervinia for weeks, staying on the route, building a mental map of every anchor, every scramble, every exposed step.

What we know about the day she vanished

Local outfitters saw her going up above the Carrel hut in the morning.
A guide on the mountain confirmed she was moving well, told the guide she was training for a record attempt, and continued upward.
She reached the summit that day. On her descent, according to friend and fellow trail runner Hillary Gerardi speaking to Outside, she vanished without a trace.

The search operation

Italian mountain rescue crews mobilized quickly.
Helicopter sweeps of the Italian face ran daily until aerial operations were suspended on September 4 after repeated flights turned up no sign of her.
Ground searches continued for several more days.
On September 8, the coordinated official search on the Matterhorn was formally called off.

The conditions this summer have been unusually severe

The Matterhorn has seen a difficult 2026 season. Heat has driven a run of rockfall events on the peak, and the route conditions have degraded significantly.
McCrystal herself had noted the route was in worse shape than it had been on her August summit.
She was, by every friend's account, aware of the conditions and taking them seriously.

Why this story matters to the running community

Skyrunning has boomed in the last few years, and the pursuit of Fastest Known Times has moved from a niche hobby onto increasingly technical terrain.
The Matterhorn round trip is now a contested objective, especially among elite women.
McCrystal is precisely the kind of athlete driving that shift: experienced, humble about the risks, and physically capable of moving fast in serious places.

The FKT calculus is changing

As speed record attempts push higher up more technical mountains, the sport is quietly having a conversation about what it is asking of its athletes.
Fastest Known Times were once the province of dirt trails and long ridges.
Now they sit on peaks that require rope work, glacier travel, and exposed climbing.
That is a different sport, and it carries different consequences.
For context on the runners currently operating at this end of the sport, our earlier piece on the biggest names missing from UTMB 2026 is a useful primer on where trail running's front row is right now. And our guide to why ultramarathon durability beats raw speed speaks to the mindset McCrystal brought to her training.

What happens now

McCrystal's family issued a statement on September 4 describing her as an experienced skyrunner and mountaineer with many years in technical high-altitude terrain.
They asked for continued support.
The formal search on the mountain has ended, but that does not mean her friends and community have stopped looking.
Squamish's mountain running community has been open about holding out hope.

A note on how this story is being reported

This is a developing situation.
Details around McCrystal's exact last known location remain limited to what the guide who saw her on the way up confirmed, and to what conditions on the mountain would allow.
This piece does not speculate on cause. It is written to sit alongside the reporting from Outside, Canadian Running Magazine, and CBC News, all of whom have followed the story with the care it deserves.
Anyone who knew Kalie McCrystal, or who follows the sport at this level, will recognize the profile immediately.
Careful, prepared, and devoted to the mountains she trained on.
The running world is holding its breath, and it will keep holding its breath for a while yet.

articles.title: Why Elite Ultrarunners Fall So Often Late in a Race, and What It Reveals About Every Runner's Body
articles.description:
When Ben Dhiman won the 2026 UTMB in 18:16:29, becoming the first man ever to break 19 hours at the race, he did it after falling hard with roughly 10 kilometres to go.
He got up, kept running, and still won by more than 31 minutes.
The fall was not bad luck. It was physics.
Elite runners fall late in long races for the same reasons recreational runners injure themselves on Sunday long runs.

The Actual Data On What Fatigue Does To A Runner

A 2016 study on a 110-kilometre mountain ultramarathon measured neuromuscular fatigue and biomechanics before and after the race.
Runners showed maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) decrements of roughly 35 percent for the knee extensors and 28 percent for the plantar flexors after the race.
That means the muscles that control landing and push-off had lost about a third of their peak force capacity.
Step frequency increased by roughly 2.7 percent as a compensatory response. Ankle range of motion decreased by around 4.1 percent.
The runners were, in effect, shuffling more than running by the end.

Why Their Bodies Chose That Strategy

The change in foot strike was fatigue-dependent, not random.
Runners who started as rearfoot strikers landed less on the heel by the end. Runners who started as forefoot strikers landed flatter.
Both groups converged on a landing pattern that minimised impact shock and muscle stretch.
It was, per the researchers, a protective adjustment.

The Postural Stability Collapse

The other reason elite runners fall late in ultras has nothing to do with muscle force.
It has to do with the sensory system that tells the brain where the body is in space.
A separate study on an 80-kilometre mountain race measured runners' postural stability with a force platform, before and after the race.
The centre-of-pressure length increased by 36 percent in the front-to-back direction and 29 percent in the side-to-side direction after the race.
In plain English: they could no longer stand still without swaying more than a third further than they had that morning.
Now translate that onto a technical descent at 10 kilometres from a UTMB finish, in the dark, on wet rocks. A fall is the expected outcome.

The Signal Recreational Runners Should Actually Take From This

Falls in long races are not a discipline problem or an attention problem.
They are the visible tip of a physiological cascade that begins hours earlier.
Every long training run does a smaller version of the same thing to a recreational body. Muscles lose force, proprioception dulls, landing changes.

What Elites Do About It, In Race

Ben Dhiman fell, got up, and finished.
Elites recover in-race for one specific reason.
Their aerobic base is deep enough that the metabolic cost of the fall itself is negligible against their remaining energy budget.
A recreational runner falling at the same relative point in a race has a much smaller cushion.
Which is why the actionable lesson is not "be more careful late".
It is "train the fatigue-resistance the elites take for granted".

The Two Training Adaptations That Matter Most

The first is single-leg strength work.
Runners who add split squats, step-downs, and single-leg deadlifts to their week show measurable improvements in late-race MVC retention.
The second is deliberate pre-fatigued balance training.
Standing on one leg with eyes closed for 30 seconds after a hard run is uncomfortable and revealing.
It also trains the same proprioceptive system that collapses in a 20-hour race.

The Injury Connection Runners Miss

The most common weekend runner injuries all cluster around the tissues that fatigue-related biomechanical changes overload.
Runner's knee tracks with quadriceps force loss and altered landing. Plantar fasciitis tracks with ankle stiffness and reduced range of motion.
The mechanism that makes an elite fall at kilometre 164 is the mechanism that gives a recreational runner a strained calf at kilometre 26.
Our full breakdown of the most common knee injuries in runners covers the front-of-knee mechanisms in detail.
And our practical exercise guide to preventing runner's knee translates the strength-work findings into a home routine.

The Trail Super-Shoe Complication

A 2025 review on ultramarathon footwear noted that current-generation trail super-shoes degrade under racing conditions.
Their functional properties change during the event itself.
Which means a shoe optimised for kilometre 50 may not be the shoe underfoot at kilometre 150. We covered how this is reshaping ultra results in our piece on
trail super-shoes rewriting who wins ultras.

What The Fall Actually Meant For Dhiman

Dhiman told reporters at the finish that the fall did not surprise him.
The surprise was that his body still had another 10 kilometres in it at that pace.
That, more than the winning time or the 45-minute margin, is the training story of his year.
It is also what separates a training block that leads to a UTMB win from one that leads to a DNF at Grand Col Ferret.
The peer-reviewed data on late-race biomechanics is available in the 110km ultramarathon fatigue study on PMC.

articles.title: Eight Months Pregnant and Still Sub-3. Ali Anderson Runs 2:59 in Sydney
articles.description:
Ali Anderson ran 2:59:43 at the Sydney Marathon on Sunday.
She is 29, from Oklahoma, and she was 32 weeks pregnant when she crossed the line.
That time puts her inside the roughly 1 percent of women who break three hours for the marathon distance.
She ran it with seventeen seconds to spare.
It was her second marathon of the pregnancy. At Boston in April, at 13 weeks, she ran a 2:41:58 personal best and announced the news afterward.

The arc from Boston to Sydney

Sydney was Anderson's seventh marathon overall and her fourth World Marathon Major. She entered before she knew she was pregnant.
Sydney's race organizers offered her a way out.
Their 2026 pregnancy and postpartum policy let a pregnant entrant defer her spot to 2027, 2028, or 2029 on a doctor's letter.
The deadline passed at 5pm AEST on August 14. She let it slide.
She told News24 Australia she saw no reason to give up the start. She joined a record 40,000 entrants running from North Sydney to the Opera House.
The pace math is worth pausing on. A sub-3 marathon requires roughly 6:51 per mile.
Anderson held that pace and little more, running about 41 seconds per mile slower than her Boston best.
She has said this is the last marathon before the birth. In her words, "I have put her through two marathons now and that is enough for her."

What the ACOG guidelines actually permit

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists updated its guidance in 2020, and it is more permissive than most people assume.
Vigorous-intensity exercise into the third trimester appears to be safe for most healthy pregnancies, according to the ACOG committee opinion. That includes running.
The guidelines also acknowledge that competitive athletes are a distinct category.
Elite athletes, defined loosely as women who train year-round at a high level, tend to maintain more strenuous training and resume high-intensity work sooner postpartum than the general population.

The caveats every pregnant runner should know

ACOG names four specific concerns for competitive athletes during pregnancy: avoiding hyperthermia, maintaining hydration, sustaining calorie intake to prevent weight loss, and staying under close medical supervision.
There is one intensity ceiling the research keeps returning to. Fetal heart rate decelerations have been reported when maternal effort exceeds roughly 90 percent of max heart rate.
Anderson's Sydney pace was under her own limit by design. She left seventeen seconds of buffer, not seventeen minutes.

What actually happens to the running body in the third trimester

Three physiological shifts define third-trimester running.
Center of gravity moves forward as the bump grows, and joint laxity increases as relaxin peaks.
The energy cost of running rises by roughly 10 to 15 percent.
None of that is dangerous, but all of it changes the effort-to-pace ratio.
That is the mechanical explanation for Anderson's roughly six-minute drop from Boston to Sydney. It was not fitness loss, it was carrying more, in a differently shaped frame, in warmer air.

What a study of 60 elite and recreational athletes actually found

A recent descriptive study followed 60 women who exercised through pregnancy above the standard guidelines. Ten were elite athletes averaging 11.6 hours of training per week, and 50 were recreational athletes at 7.0 hours per week.
Most resumed exercise within six weeks postpartum.
Most had spontaneous onset of labor and vaginal deliveries at term.
The mean birthweight was 3,487 grams, which is inside the normal healthy range.
Two of the elite athletes were diagnosed with gestational diabetes and two with hypertension during pregnancy.
None of the 50 recreational athletes reported any pregnancy complications. The full paper is available on PMC for anyone who wants the primary data.

The course she ran on

The Sydney Marathon course is not gentle. It carries 313 meters of climbing against a net drop of 83 meters, which converts to roughly 1,027 feet up and 272 feet down.
That is more vertical than most World Marathon Majors offer.
Anderson also ran it in her seventh marathon start, on a body carrying an extra 20 or so pounds of gestational weight.
A closer look at what the course actually demands sits in this breakdown of why Sydney is now the hardest of the World Marathon Majors.

What she is not claiming, and what she is

Anderson is not claiming pregnant women should race marathons.
She is not a physiologist and her interviews have been careful.
What she is doing is quieter. She is showing that the assumption of complete rest through pregnancy, still the default advice most women get, is not what the current medical guidelines actually say for someone who was already training at a high level going in.
She had a third marathon booked for December and had planned an attempt at the American Olympic Marathon Trials standard. USATF has set that at 2:37:00 for women in 2028.
Her Boston time sits 4 minutes and 58 seconds outside it.
She has time.

The wider category she now belongs in

Anderson is not the first athlete to race deep into a pregnancy, and she will not be the last.
The precedents span every distance from track to ultra.
What makes her case land differently is the specificity of the numbers: a 2:59:43 at 32 weeks, five months after a 2:41:58 personal best at 13 weeks.
That is a training log, not an anecdote.
She joins a small but growing catalog of runners who have stayed inside their own effort envelope while their body changed around them
It is the same envelope, on a different scale, that shapes what happens to running after 40, or what a marathon looks like at 90.

The finish line she actually crossed

The clock in the Sydney Opera House forecourt read 2:59:43 as Anderson came through.
She had entered the race before she knew she was pregnant.
She raced it anyway, stayed inside the guidelines she was working with, and left the door open on a Trials standard she has almost three years to chase.
Seventeen seconds under three hours, at 32 weeks, on a course most people find punishing sober.
That is the story, and the story does not require any interpretation to land.

articles.title: Julien Veysseyre Crossed the UTMB Finish Line on One Leg and Made History
articles.description:
Picture from HOKA UTMB Mont Blanc
Shortly after 4 p.m. on Sunday, Julien Veysseyre walked under the finish arch in Chamonix with his children beside him and became the first amputee ever to finish the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc.
Official timing places the 39-year-old Frenchman 1,475th in 44 hours, 16 minutes, 4 seconds, on the 173.6km loop with about 9,700 meters of climbing.

What The 44 Hours Actually Cost Him

Veysseyre lost his right leg to a workplace accident at 18.
He came to trail running through triathlon, where he was crowned world para-triathlon champion in 2023, before Salomon brought him onto its para team.
Last year he finished the CCC, the 100km sister race to UTMB. This year he came for the main event.
A below-knee amputee uses roughly 10 to 30 percent more metabolic energy to walk than a runner with two biological legs, per a 2018 paper in Scientific Reports.
Running on a blade adds socket friction. It loads the sound side harder, and it changes gait on every technical step.
Now stretch that penalty across 174 kilometers of alpine trail and roughly two full nights of movement.

Five Guides. Two Prosthetics. One Route.

Veysseyre did not go alone.
Five pacers rotated through the two nights on the mountain. Part of what they carried was a
second prosthesis, swapped in as the terrain changed, according to AFP.
La Montagne tracked his stops and counted just 1 hour, 59 minutes, 16 seconds off his feet across the entire race.
That included two longer breaks of 37 and 40 minutes, one on each night.
The rest of it was motion.

The Course Itself Was Not The One Runners Signed Up For

UTMB organizers pushed the start two hours late on Friday, from 5:45 p.m. to 7:45 p.m., over a thunderstorm risk on the ridge line.
They also cut the Pyramides Calcaires section out of the route, shortening the loop and adjusting the final cutoff to 6:30 p.m. on Sunday.
Veysseyre reached that finish arch with roughly 2 hours, 25 minutes of cutoff time still on the clock.
Race winner Ben Dhiman had been done for a full day by then, breaking 19 hours in the process.
You can look up the full winning story of the 2026 field in our coverage of Kilian Jornet's return campaign and the men's field.
Pictures from HOKA UTMB Mont Blanc

Why This Result Sits Outside The Official Rankings

UTMB does not run a para classification.
That means Veysseyre's name appears in the standard M4 (35-39) men's category, mixed in with every non-amputee runner in his age group.
There is no adjusted time, no separate podium, no asterisk in the results file.
The result is a plain finish, ranked against every other finisher.
Which, given what covering that ground actually costs a single-leg athlete, is the point.

The Field Was Not A Small One

Roughly 2,400 runners left the Place du Triangle de l'Amitié on Friday evening.
Many of the biggest names in the sport were not among them. We laid out the headline absences from the 2026 UTMB elite field earlier this year.
Their absence did not shrink what Veysseyre did. If anything, the story that walked under the arch on Sunday afternoon was the story of the weekend.

The Champagne In The Prosthesis

One image made the rounds in French sports coverage on Sunday night.
Veysseyre poured champagne into his racing blade at the finish and drank from it in front of his crew.
The gesture was small. The subtext was the point.
A device that once defined what he had lost was, on Sunday, the thing he was celebrating from.

What Comes Next For Him

Veysseyre has said the UTMB was the biggest challenge he would ever attempt.
He described the finish, in mixed zone, in the language of someone still trying to believe it.
The scale of the reception surprised him. By his own account, most of the runners still out on the mountain knew his first name.
A single UTMB result does not create a para category on its own.
It does, however, make one harder to argue against.
Every future amputee entrant now has an actual finish to point at, in an actual results file, with an actual bib number.
The ceiling moved on Sunday afternoon. Somebody had to move it first.
Veysseyre had spent three years preparing for a single objective.
He had built through the para-triathlon world title and the CCC 100km as staging posts, not as end points.
Whether he returns to the Chamonix start line is an open question. Whether other amputee entrants will now line up behind him is not.
The full context of the run, including guide rotations and split analysis, is documented in Marathon Handbook's finish-line report.
The metabolic-cost figure comes from an open-access study on lower-limb amputee locomotion hosted on PMC.

articles.title: At 90, a Retired Doctor Just Became the Oldest Person Ever to Climb Kilimanjaro
articles.description:
Courtesy World Wide Trekking

His name is Dr. Art Ulene, and the walk lasted 15 days.
At the top, standing at roughly 19,341 feet, he ate birthday cake. Then he danced.
That summit made him the oldest human known to have climbed the highest mountain in Africa.

The record he broke, and the one he was chasing

The prior record belonged to Anne Lorimor, an American who summited Kilimanjaro in July 2019 at 89 years and 37 days.
The Lorimor record was officially recognised by Guinness. The Ulene claim, at 90 years exactly, awaits Guinness verification.
That verification typically takes up to three months, per Guinness policy. The National Park Service reportedly had a representative on the mountain to witness the summit.
According to reporting by Alaska News Source, the ascent was confirmed the same day by his daughter, Dr. Valerie Ulene.

Who Dr. Art Ulene actually is

Ulene is a retired OB-GYN. He is also, for a certain generation of American viewers, a familiar television face.
He served for years as the medical correspondent on the NBC TODAY show, translating clinical research into practical advice for a huge audience.
That professional background is not decorative. It is the entire reason he framed this climb the way he did.

The frame he keeps using in every interview

In a conversation with NPR before the trip, Ulene laid out the sentence every runner and every ageing athlete should copy down.
Most people, he said, worry about their lifespan. Smart people worry about their healthspan, which is how many of those years are spent in good health.
His stated ambition is for the two numbers to be equal, meaning he wants to be in the best possible health right up to the last day.
Kilimanjaro was the loudest way he could think of to make that argument in public.
Courtesy of CareScout

The climb itself, in his own words

This was not a heroic sprint up the mountain.
The full trip took 15 days.
Eleven and a half of those were spent going up. Four were spent coming down.
The group carried a folding chair for him. Roughly every hour, they set it up and he sat for five to 10 minutes to recover.
He told The Spokesman-Review that his legs simply would not go any faster and that pace, not fitness, was the ceiling.

The hardest part was not what most people assume

Ulene has said the hardest part of the climb was not the altitude or the cold.
It was lifting himself over large rocks on the technical sections. The descent was almost as tough, because a 90-year-old body has to actively brake every step to avoid tumbling.
His summit line, remembered afterwards, is the one worth repeating. He kept telling himself that all he had to do was put one foot in front of the other.
That is not a motivational poster. That is the mechanical reality of ultra-endurance at any age.

This was not his first Kilimanjaro

Ulene had climbed the mountain twice before.
The first time was in 2011, at 75, with his wife Priscilla. She was 72.
He attempted it again in a subsequent year and turned back before the summit. That returned attempt is why the 90th-birthday climb was not a first-time act, but a settled score.
The relevant lesson for older runners is quiet but important.
Attempts that end short of the goal are not failures. They are altitude acclimatisation for the future.

Why this belongs on a running website

Ulene is not a distance runner in any formal sense. He is a doctor, a skier, and now a record-holding climber.
